raw_case_text:
A 43 year old man with no history of chronic illness was well until the day of presentation when he had an episode of seizure. While the patient was asleep, his relative noted stiffening of his body followed rapidly by rhythmic jerking of all his limbs which lasted about 45 s. He was unresponsive to calls during the episode. There was no fecal or urinary incontinence or foaming at the mouth. He had had two similar episodes of generalized seizures in the preceding 12 months. He was admitted at a clinic when he had the first seizure but was subsequently lost to follow-up. There was no family history of epilepsy and he had never traveled outside of Ghana. He was a non-smoker and also drank alcohol occasionally but did not use illicit drugs. He was a regular pork eater and a previous pig farmer. He lived in a community with free-ranging pigs and limited access to toilet facilities. On arrival at the emergency unit of our hospital, he had another episode of generalized seizure which was aborted with intravenous diazepam.
On physical examination, he was afebrile (37.1 C), anicteric, not pale, not dyspnoeic, and not wasted. There was no tongue bite, oral thrush or peripheral lymphadenopathy. Random blood sugar was 6.6 mmol/L. He had a regular pulse of 63 beats per minute and a blood pressure of 117/63 mmHg. He was fully conscious with no obvious neurologic deficit. His neck was supple with negative Kernig's sign.
Laboratory investigations revealed normal complete blood count, renal and liver biochemistries, serum electrolytes (Ca2+, Mg2+, Na+, K+) and negative HIV status. Contrast enhanced CT scan of the head showed rim-enhancing, cystic lesions with eccentric internal hyperdense foci in both frontal lobes (Figure 3). There was no perilesional edema. Also noted was a calcified cortical nodule in the left parietal region (Figure 4).
A diagnosis of vesicular and calcified stages of parenchymal neurocysticercosis was made. Ocular cysticercosis and papilledema were ruled out with funduscopic assessment. Anti-seizure treatment with levetiracetam was initiated. He was also started on a 2 week course of albendazole together with dexamethasone which was started 24 h before initiation of albendazole therapy. At follow-up 2 months after discharge, there had been no recurrence of seizures.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 43-year-old Ghanaian man presented to the emergency unit following a witnessed 45-second nocturnal generalized tonic-clonic seizure.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: While asleep on the day of presentation, his relative observed body stiffening rapidly followed by rhythmic jerking of all four limbs lasting approximately 45 seconds, during which he was unresponsive to calls. There was no foaming at the mouth or urinary/fecal incontinence. Upon arrival at the hospital emergency unit, he experienced a second generalized seizure that was aborted with intravenous diazepam.
subjective.past_medical_history: No history of chronic medical illness, no family history of epilepsy, and no travel outside Ghana. He had experienced two similar generalized seizures over the preceding 12 months and was admitted to a local clinic after the first episode before being lost to follow-up. He was a former pig farmer and regular pork consumer living in a community with free-ranging pigs and limited toilet facilities. He did not smoke or use illicit drugs and drank alcohol occasionally.
subjective.review_of_systems: Negative for fecal or urinary incontinence and foaming at the mouth.

objective.physical_examination: He was afebrile (37.1 °C), fully conscious, anicteric, not pale, not dyspneic, and not wasted, with a regular pulse of 63 bpm and blood pressure of 117/63 mmHg. There was no tongue bite, oral thrush, or peripheral lymphadenopathy. Neck was supple with a negative Kernig's sign, and neurological and funduscopic examinations revealed no focal deficits, papilledema, or ocular cysticercosis.
objective.routine_investigations: Random blood glucose was 6.6 mmol/L. Complete blood count, renal and liver biochemistries, serum electrolytes (Ca2+, Mg2+, Na+, K+), and HIV status were all normal/negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Contrast-enhanced head CT demonstrated bilateral frontal lobe rim-enhancing cystic lesions containing eccentric internal hyperdense foci (scolices) without perilesional edema, along with a calcified cortical nodule in the left parietal region.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Parenchymal neurocysticercosis in the vesicular and calcified stages was confirmed by characteristic head CT findings showing cysts with eccentric scolices and a parietal calcified nodule. Acute seizure activity was aborted with IV diazepam, and maintenance levetiracetam was initiated alongside a 2-week course of albendazole and dexamethasone (started 24 hours prior to albendazole). At 2-month post-discharge follow-up, he had no recurrence of seizures.
